summary: Crossing the Sea of Galilee at evening, Jesus sleeps through a violent storm, then rebukes the wind and waves, and His terrified disciples ask who He is.
key_insight: The disciples were afraid in the storm, but Mark says that after the calm “they feared exceedingly.” Facing the wind, they feared for their lives; facing Jesus, they feared the One whom even the wind and sea obey.
story: That same day, when evening came, {Mk} Jesus saw the great crowds around Him and gave orders to cross to the other side. {Mt} A scribe came and said, “Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.” Jesus answered, “Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.” Another disciple said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” Jesus replied, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” {Mt}
They left the crowd and took Him along in the boat just as He was, and other little boats went with Him. {Mk} As they sailed, He fell asleep. {Lk}

Suddenly a great windstorm came down on the lake. {Lk} The waves beat into the boat until it was already filling, {Mk} and they were in danger. {Lk} But Jesus was in the stern, asleep on a pillow. {Mk}
They woke Him, crying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” {Mt} “Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?” {Mk}

He arose and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace, be still!” The wind ceased, and there was a great calm. {Mk} Then He said to them, “Why are you so fearful? How is it that you have no faith?” {Mk}
They were filled with fear and amazement and said to one another, “Who can this be? For He commands even the winds and water, and they obey Him!” {Lk}
differences: Only Matthew records the two would-be followers before the crossing; Luke tells a similar exchange later, on the road toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:57–60).
Matthew places the storm before the parables of chapter 13. Mark dates it “On the same day” as the parables, “when evening had come.”
The disciples cry, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” (Matthew), “Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?” (Mark) and “Master, Master, we are perishing!” (Luke).
In Matthew, Jesus questions their faith before He calms the sea; in Mark and Luke, after. Luke’s question is “Where is your faith?”
Only Mark mentions the other boats, the stern, the pillow and the words “Peace, be still!”

fit.question: Matthew tells the storm in chapter 8, long before the parables of chapter 13. Mark says it happened on the evening of the day of parables. Which is right?

points.label: Matthew groups by theme
points.text: Matthew 8–9 gathers ten mighty works to show the King’s authority over disease, nature, demons, sin and death. He does not say when the storm happened, only that it followed a time of great crowds (8:18).

points.label: Mark gives the time
points.text: Mark ties the crossing to the parables: “On the same day, when evening had come” (4:35). Luke’s “on a certain day” leaves the time open. Mark’s note is the clearest guide to the order.

points.label: The would-be followers
points.text: Matthew sets these sayings before the crossing; Luke has similar words later (Luke 9:57–62). Jesus may have said such things more than once, or Matthew placed them here because they fit his theme: right after them, “His disciples followed Him” into the boat (8:23).

fit.note: Matthew arranges by subject and Mark by sequence; both report real events truthfully.
fit.short: Matthew groups his miracles by theme in chapters 8–9; Mark gives the time, the evening after the parables.

fit.question: Did Jesus rebuke the disciples’ fear before He calmed the storm (Matthew) or after (Mark and Luke)? And which words did the disciples cry out?

points.label: Many voices in a sinking boat
points.text: Frightened men in a filling boat do not speak in one sentence. “Save us,” “do You not care” and “Master, Master” are the kinds of cries several men would shout at once, and each Gospel preserves one.

points.label: Words before and after
points.text: Jesus may well have spoken about their fear as He rose and again once the sea was still. Matthew puts the rebuke first; Mark and Luke place it after the calm.

fit.note: The witnesses agree on everything that matters: the storm, the sleeping Lord, the cry, the command, the calm and the question of faith.
fit.short: Several frightened men shouted different words. Jesus may have spoken about their faith both as He rose and after the calm.

scene.label: Sudden storms
scene.text: The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level, ringed by hills and cut by steep valleys. Cool air from the heights can rush down onto the warm water with little warning and raise high waves in minutes.

scene.label: A fishing boat
scene.text: In 1986 a first-century boat was found in the mud near Magdala. It was about 27 feet long and 7½ feet wide and could carry perhaps fifteen people. Boats like it probably had a small raised deck at the stern, where a tired man could lie down.

scene.label: Jonah’s storm
scene.text: Jonah also slept through a storm at sea, until the ship’s captain woke him and begged him to call on his God, “so that we may not perish” (Jonah 1:6). There the sea grew calm when Jonah was thrown overboard; here it grows calm at Jesus’ word.

scene.label: Only God rules the sea
scene.text: The psalms praise the Lord who rules “the raging of the sea” and “calms the storm, So that its waves are still” (Psalm 89:9; 107:29). The disciples’ question rises from songs they had known since childhood.

witnesses.matthew: Sets the storm among the King’s mighty works and frames it with discipleship: would-be followers, then “His disciples followed Him” into the boat. Their cry, “Lord, save us!”, reads like a prayer, and “O you of little faith” is a phrase Matthew records four times.
witnesses.mark: Gives the eyewitness touches: evening, the other boats, Jesus asleep on a pillow in the stern, and the blunt “do You not care?” Jesus’ command to the sea uses the same word He spoke to silence a demon in Capernaum (Mark 1:25), as if the storm were an enemy to be muzzled.
witnesses.luke: Tells it briefly but stresses the danger: they “were in jeopardy.” Luke’s Jesus asks, “Where is your faith?”, a question that assumes they had faith and had not used it.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is truly human, tired enough to sleep through a storm, and truly divine, speaking to wind and sea as their Maker. The disciples’ question has only one answer in Israel’s Scriptures: the Lord.
seeing.living: Jesus did not keep the storm away, but He was in the boat the whole time. He does not scold them for feeling the wind; He asks where their faith is. Bring Him the honest cry, “Lord, save us!”, and let His answer turn fear of the storm into awe of Him.
seeing.ponder: In the storm you are facing now, are you more aware of the waves or of who is in the boat with you?

preaching.big_idea: The storm exposes our fear; the calm reveals who Jesus is.
outline: A storm and a sleeping Savior (37–38)
A word that stilled the sea (39–40)
A greater fear and the right question (41)
preaching.watch_for: This is the first of four mighty works in Mark 4:35–5:43: over a storm, a legion of demons, a long illness and death itself. Read together, they show that nothing lies outside Jesus’ authority.
